Then , the rupee was fixed for a considerable period based on motivations that were obscure , perhaps unsavoury , in favouring large foreign currency borrowers ( Figure 1 ) . The fixity worsened the competitiveness of the economy and was only sustained by a loss of over $150 billion in valuable reserves . In the end , it provoked a speculative attack against a rupee that had become clearly over-valued @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ last one year , the new RBI regime has managed the rupee better and more flexibly . There is the important question of why foreign capital is bolting out of India when , in fact , there ought to be a stampede into the country if the economy is supposedly growing at a torrid 8.2 per cent , much faster than any comparable country . In the event , the RBI has partially allowed this capital flight to be reflected in the exchange rate , which has declined from 85 rupees to the dollar to 90 rupees to the dollar over the last year . " <p> -- " Second , however , old habits persist . From the middle of 2025 , when pressures on the rupee re-emerged for a host of external ( Trump tariffs , investor re-assessment in favour of China ) and domestic reasons ( weak private investment and doubts about official growth numbers ) , the RBI started intervening again to partially defend the rupee . Based on official data and some estimates for November and December , it seems that since June 2025 , @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ the extent of $30-35 billion and may have intervened in the forward market to the extent of up to $30 billion . " <p> -- " This raises the question : Why , oh why ? Losing reserves to prevent high inflation is one thing but doing so when there is no such risk is damaging . One might speculate that there are two interest groups arguing against a rupee decline . First are those Indians who have dollar expenditures , including large companies that have borrowed in dollars , and middle class and rich households who want to send their children abroad for education . The second group are nationalist politicians for whom a declining rupee is a sign of weakness . " <p> -- " The response of policy-makers to the former group must be to highlight the plight of the tens of millions of workers in labour-intensive industries ( fisheries , gems and jewellery , and clothing ) all across the country who have lost or are at risk of losing their jobs and livelihoods because of the devastating Trump tariffs . It is undeniable that the @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ instance , a weaker rupee protects millions of the poor , while a strong rupee favours the rich few . " <p> -- " The reality is that protecting the job-intensive export sector requires a much weaker currency . How much weaker ? Take some illustrative calculations . Figure 2 shows that India 's real exchange rate has declined relative to the average of the last five years by about 5 per cent while China 's has by about 12 per cent . An alternative calculation is that India has been burdened by a punitive Trump tariff of 25 per cent ( over and above competitor countries ) . " <p> -- " Whether India needs to catch up with Chinese competitiveness or needs an exchange rate to offset the punitive tariffs , a further 10 per cent decline in the rupee seems almost necessary , especially given that there has been very little fiscal support from the government . " <p> -- " The irony is that markets are trying to do a desirable job that policy makers have themselves been unable or unwilling to ( a rupee depreciation is effectively a subsidy to exporters ) ; instead of sitting back and availing themselves of the benefits , vested interests and politicians are actually thwarting markets to the detriment of the economy . This is self-inflicted damage . Also , the government should allow the RBI to manage a truly flexible exchange rate policy because it is undertaking a number of desirable reforms whose impact can be magnified and brought forward by a more competitive currency . " <p> Do You Know : <p> -- The rate at which one can swap between currencies is the exchange rate . This is , arguably , the most significant privacy reform since the IT Act , 2000 . The DPDP Act , along with the Rules , aims to foster respect for individual rights and data accountability . " <p> -- What are the key features of the Digital Personal Data Protection Act ? <p> -- What is data localisation ? <p> -- Who are data fiduciaries ? <p> -- Why is there a need for data protection law ? <p> -- Which other countries have data protection laws ? <p> -- What are the @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ : <p> -- " It will impact the healthcare sector in a big way . As with most ambitious reforms , the devil lurks in the details . The Act elevates every clinic , hospital , lab and telemedicine app to the category of " data fiduciary " . It does not differentiate between a large hospital , a small clinic , a large corporation , or a start-up . " <p> -- " Any personal data in digital form , or in non-digital form and digitised later , is subject to the Act ( unless it falls in the limited exceptions in Section 3(c) of the Act ) . Patients become " data principals " with rights to access , correct and even erase their medical information . On paper , this is empowering . In practice , Indian healthcare now finds itself navigating a maze where the law is clear about duties , but vague about the boundaries . " <p> -- " Anyone who has signed a hospital consent form knows that it is quite often an exercise in blind faith rather than informed choice . The @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ Act , with the laudable objective of minimising data collection and retention , gives a wide berth to the individual to withdraw consent or to seek deletion of data . While this may be relevant for sectors such as online gaming or e-commerce , it creates complications for the healthcare sector . " <p> -- " If a patient withdraws consent , or if there is a request to erase personal data , the fiduciary is bound to delete the said data and stop " processing " it . However , who is to take the responsibility for the treatment and health of such a patient ? The Act does warn the data principal that it will be the individual who will be responsible for the consequences of the withdrawal of consent . But it is worth remembering that the DPDP Act does not take away the legal obligations of the healthcare sector . " <p> -- " The definition of " processing " in the Act includes " erasure " and " destruction " . This unusual idea that none , including Planck , believed in at that time was , however , successful in describing thermal radiation . " <p> -- " In 1905 , Albert Einstein picked it up to explain the photoelectric effect . In 1913 , Niels Bohr applied it to decode the hydrogen atom . All these were quick-fix solutions without a coherent story . In @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ into one cohesive framework . " <p> -- " Throughout the 1920s , many other scientists were working to decode the quantum puzzle . In 1924 , French physicist Louis de Broglie proposed in his doctoral thesis that material particles , such as electrons and protons , can behave like waves . This was so radical that his doctoral committee remained unconvinced , but finally yielded when Einstein stated that deBroglie had " lifted a corner of the great veil " . Building on this picture , in 1925 , the Austrian physicist Erwin Schr ? dinger developed a wave equation that now bears his name . This landmark equation made it easier to apply quantum principles to subatomic particles and even the whole universe . " <p> -- " In 1924 , Satyendra Nath Bose , then working in Calcutta , wrote to Einstein about his method of counting photons . Einstein recognised the novelty and expanded its scope leading to the prediction of a new state of matter , the Bose -- Einstein condensate , which was observed decades later . " <p> -- " C V Raman @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ quantum effects in light-matter interactions , earning him the 1930 Nobel Prize . Thanks to these developments , semiconductors emerged in the 1950s , lasers in the 1960s , high-density hard disks in the 1990s , and sensing devices in the 2000s . This is a story of how investment in basic sciences returns dividends for over a century . The governments must resist the urge to cut funds for basic research . The danger is especially acute when classifications are based on race , nationality , or religion . <p> One of the most alarming examples of this misuse of classification is the approach of colonisers and foreign occupying powers toward the resistance of occupied peoples . @@132939367 <h> From Polemic to Peace : A Palestinian Christian Hermeneutic of Justice and Inclusive Hope in the Israeli-Palestinian Conflict <h> Share : <p> Jamie Glazov 's essay , " Tucker Carlson 's Lies About Israel , " published on FrontPage Mag on October 30 , 2025 , extends beyond a mere journalistic critique ; it functions as a meticulously crafted polemic , strategically employing moral , theological , and overtly dehumanizing language to defend the State of Israel 's policies against critical scrutiny , as personified by Carlson . This text is not an objective journalistic endeavour ; it is a performative act of ideological warfare , aiming to cement a particular narrative while discrediting all opposing viewpoints . At its core , Glazov 's argument is two-fold : first , it posits that Israel demonstrates " unprecedented moral efforts " by purportedly valuing Palestinian life , while simultaneously reducing Palestinian national identity to a monolithic " death cult " rooted in Islam . The essay immediately opens by branding Carlson 's critique of Israel as a " vicious and grotesque lie , " setting a stark truth-lie dichotomy that positions Glazov as the authoritative arbiter of moral truth . The defence of Israel 's actions rests on a circular logic of moral exceptionalism : Israel " sees Palestinians as human , " a claim ostensibly proven by the IDF tactical sacrifices , such as " going door-to-door in searches instead of carpet bombing . " This narrative attempts to immunize the state 's conduct from any substantial criticism by exclusively foregrounding its military process rather than engaging with the profound human and political outcomes of the prolonged occupation and incessant conflict . <p> From a justice perspective , this argument is structurally flawed and inherently misleading . @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ territorial occupation , systematic dispossession , and the continuous denial of Palestinian self-determination -- factors that are unequivocally the root causes of political violence . Instead , Glazov artfully reframes the entire conflict solely as a confrontation between an ethically superior military and a barbaric " death cult . " This discursive manoeuvre serves to externalize all moral culpability entirely onto the Palestinian side , effectively absolving Israel of any responsibility for the structural conditions that fuel the conflict . Furthermore , Glazov 's assertion that Hamas uses human shields " KNOWING that Israel values Palestinian lives " is a highly charged and deeply problematic assumption . It disingenuously shifts complete responsibility for the casualties of war entirely onto the victimized population and their representatives , rather than acknowledging the inherent responsibilities of the occupying power or the complexities of urban warfare . This rhetorical move is designed to deflect moral scrutiny from Israel 's actions . <p> Perhaps most disturbingly , the essay explicitly dehumanizes the Palestinian people by reducing their entire socio-political identity to a state of being " brainwashed and indoctrinated " from birth . This rhetorical @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ an innate , culturally mandated truth rather than a possible , understandable response to generations of historical injustice and ongoing oppression , serves several insidious functions : it denies Palestinians political agency , stripping them of their fundamental capacity to make rational political choices or articulate grievances ; it fosters theological othering , transforming a complex ethno-national conflict into a timeless , irreconcilable religious war ; and it justifies severity , implicitly sanctioning the harshest security measures against an existential evil , thereby undermining any legitimate call for restorative justice . Such dehumanization , as scholars like Edward Said ( 1978 ) have meticulously demonstrated , is a prerequisite for colonial domination , transforming the colonized into an undifferentiated , threatening mass devoid of individual humanity and legitimate grievances . <p> We should remember that since October 7 , 2023 , Israel 's military offensive in Gaza has caused a catastrophic humanitarian disaster . The sheer scale of destruction , with over 70,000 tons of explosives dropped and 70% of homes damaged or destroyed , points to a systematic crisis of deprivation , bombardment , and blockade . The human cost challenges the claim of moral restraint , highlighting a profound historical atrocity . <p> Failure of Interreligious Inclusion <p> Glazov 's polemic relies heavily on a selective , essentializing , and profoundly decontextualized hermeneutics of Islam . Yet , as trauma scholars like Judith Butler ( 2009 ) and Ilan Gur-Ze'ev ( 2005 ) profoundly note , such rhetoric instrumentalizes suffering not to foster healing or understanding , but to justify perpetual warfare and retribution . The citation of atrocities occurring outside the immediate context of Palestine functions to universalize Islam 's perceived guilt and to distract from Israel 's moral accountability within the conflict zone . Yet , the suffering of Christians in other contexts , however real and tragic , can not ethically justify the oppression of Muslims or Christians elsewhere . Moral universality demands consistency and non-selectivity : if the dignity and human rights of Christians in Pakistan must be defended , then with equal moral fervour , the dignity and human rights of Muslims and Christians under occupation in Gaza and the West Bank must also be defended . <p> The Crisis of Truth and the Imperative of Interreligious Hermeneutics <p> The deeper crisis revealed by @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ traditions are weaponized to sacralise political power and justify state violence , truth becomes the first and most tragic casualty . Interreligious hermeneutics -- the comparative , dialogical , and empathetic reading of sacred texts across traditions -- offers a crucial antidote to this ideological closure and the distortion of truth . In both Islamic and Christian traditions , divine revelation is never presented as a warrant for domination or oppression . The Quran ( 5:32 ) unequivocally upholds the sanctity of all human life , proclaiming that " whoever kills a soul unless for a soul or for corruption done in the land -- it is as if he had slain mankind entirely . And whoever saves one -- it is as if he had saved mankind entirely . " Similarly , the Gospel ( John 10:10 ) proclaims that Christ came " that they may have life , and have it abundantly . " These profound texts , when read inclusively and with genuine hermeneutical integrity , converge on a moral vision of universal human flourishing and the inherent sanctity of every life . <p> To restore this @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ scripture not through the narrow , divisive lens of exclusivism , but through the expansive and healing hermeneutics of compassion and justice . Interfaith scholars such as Hans Kung ( 2007 ) and Farid Esack powerfully argue that global peace is inextricably dependent on recovering the moral unity that lies beneath apparent religious plurality -- a unity rooted in fundamental justice , not in supremacy or domination . From a Palestinian Christian and global humanist perspective , the true theological question is not whether Israel 's wars are morally justified , but rather , whether any theology that sanctifies oppression , dispossession , and violence can credibly still speak of God , who is often understood as a God of justice , love , and mercy for all . Glazov 's essay , through its distortions , exemplifies a profound theological failure in this regard . This failure to embody the core ethical teachings of their respective faiths is precisely what hinders genuine interreligious dialogue and reconciliation . <p> Critical Reflection on Power , Narrative , and Structural Injustice <p> The essay 's framing hinges on a powerful moral and @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ ( and by extension , the broader Palestinian identity ) as inherently villainous . While this narrative purports to uphold justice , it regrettably risks profoundly marginalizing the legitimate narratives of Palestinian suffering and resistance . From a different hermeneutical standpoint -- one rooted in liberation theology and critical postcolonial studies -- Palestinian struggle can be understood as rooted in a deeply felt quest for justice against persistent dispossession and occupation . From a critical hermeneutical lens oriented towards liberation and interfaith dialogue , it is vital to recognize how power dynamics and dominant narratives profoundly shape what is perceived as " truth . " The prevailing discourse , as exemplified by Glazov 's essay , often dangerously simplifies complex realities . For example , it reduces the multifaceted conflict to a simplistic , binary morality where one side is inherently righteous and the other inherently villainous . Such framing tragically perpetuates cycles of mistrust , dehumanization , and violent conflict , thereby actively hindering the possibility of genuine peace and reconciliation . <p> A more nuanced and ethically responsible hermeneutic advocates for understanding and acknowledging multiple narratives , recognizing @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ Palestinian Christians , while simultaneously affirming Israel 's undeniable right to security . This balanced approach encourages interpreting biblical , historical , and contemporary narratives through the lenses of justice , compassion , and reconciliation , rather than through condemnation , demonization , or tribalistic triumphalism . Furthermore , the text constructs Israel 's military actions as moral heroism -- claiming that soldiers " sacrifice their lives to spare Palestinian lives . " This narrative of moral exceptionalism dangerously obscures the profound asymmetry of power in the conflict and the systematic nature of occupation : the pervasive control of land , water resources , movement , and economic life for millions of Palestinians . In framing Israel as engaged solely in reluctant self-defence , the essay reproduces what political theologian Marc Ellis ( 1987 ) calls the " myth of innocent power , " wherein violence perpetrated by the powerful is moralized as necessary and redemptive , effectively masking its oppressive nature . This critical analysis underscores that structural injustice can not be redressed through narratives that deny its very existence or systematically blame the oppressed . <p> Toward a @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ ethically grounded hermeneutic must holistically incorporate both the biblical promises to Israel and the universal prophetic call for justice , mercy , and comprehensive peace . It passionately advocates for reading sacred texts not solely as instruments of identity or exclusion , but primarily as profound sources of moral inspiration for overcoming division and fostering genuine reconciliation . Such an approach suggests that Christian , Jewish , and Muslim faith communities share a common divine calling : to actively pursue justice , to seek reconciliation with perceived enemies , and to foster enduring peace . Recognizing the profound shared heritage and divine mandates rooted in Abrahamic scriptures reinforces the urgent and undeniable need for dialogue grounded in mutual respect , radical empathy , and divine justice . Theologically , this approach challenges Christian communities to see their role as ardent advocates for a peace that deeply embodies biblical principles -- justice as rooted in the divine character , unconditional love for neighbour ( including the enemy ) , and the absolute sacredness of every human life . This necessarily involves rejecting narratives that dehumanize or dismiss the suffering of others @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ profound reconciliation . <p> In understanding the complex dynamics articulated in Glazov 's essay , it becomes abundantly clear that faith , when interpreted hermeneutically with justice , profound compassion , and genuine humility , can indeed serve as a transformative force in authentic peacebuilding . The Christian theological perspective , particularly as articulated by Palestinian liberation theologians , strongly emphasizes that the moral imperatives of Scripture -- justice , mercy , and love -- are not mere suggestions but are essential , non-negotiable guides for ethically engaging with the Israeli-Palestinian conflict . Glazov 's discourse , while impassioned , hermeneutically distorts realities to sustain a pro-Israel hegemony , fostering division over peace . From a Palestinian Christian vantage , it exemplifies " cheap grace " ( Dietrich Bonhoeffer ) , excusing injustice under a veneer of religious justification . True interreligious justice demands a bold reckoning : dismantling occupation , pursuing equitable two-state or confederal solutions , and embracing inclusive dialogues that genuinely extend the spirit of peace equitably to all . Only through such profound hermeneutical humility and courageous truth-telling can global peace truly emerge , honouring the @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ his selective application , ultimately undermines . <p> Reclaiming Shared Foundations <p> The essay 's emphasis on biblical roots and specific Christian theological commitments , while intended to bolster a particular narrative , ironically opens a vital hermeneutical pathway for interfaith dialogue aimed at authentic peace and reconciliation . Recognizing that Jesus , the central figure of Christianity , was deeply rooted in Jewish customs , observed the Sabbath , celebrated Passover , and revered the Temple , firmly links Christianity to Judaism -- not as a break or replacement , but as a profound continuation and spiritual fulfilment of biblical promises . This fundamental understanding underscores the critical importance of acknowledging the continuity between the covenantal promises to Israel and Christian salvation history , fostering mutual respect and genuine solidarity between faith communities . From a hermeneutic of mutual recognition , such acknowledgment can serve as an indispensable foundation for bridging deep divides . Interfaith dialogue that emphasizes shared sacred history -- the Abrahamic traditions , the profound significance of Jerusalem , and common ethical imperatives such as justice , compassion , and human dignity -- can actively foster @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ This perspective aligns powerfully with Christian theology 's call for radical love of neighbour and the relentless pursuit of justice , extending these principles to Palestinians and Israelis alike , without selectivity or prejudice . It invites believers to interpret their faith 's teachings as promoting not loss or conquest , but rather profound reconciliation , universal dignity , and divine justice . Such an inclusive hermeneutic is absolutely vital for constructing narratives that heal wounds , mourn collective losses , and ultimately uphold the inherent human dignity of all . <p> The Role of Palestinian Christians and Their Theological Voices <p> Crucially , this analysis continuously brings to light the essential Palestinian Christian perspective , which is often marginalized or entirely erased in mainstream debates , including Glazov 's essay . Palestinian Christians -- believers deeply rooted in biblical faith -- stand uniquely at the intersection of faith , justice , and political resistance . Their voices , emphasizing their own profound suffering and their distinctive theological understanding of justice , demand recognition within the wider interfaith and geopolitical dialogues . From a hermeneutical standpoint , Palestinian Christian theology @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ justice . It emphasizes motifs such as the Exodus ( God 's liberation of the oppressed ) , solidarity with the marginalized , and the prophetic call to righteousness ( e.g. , Amos 5:24 : " But let justice roll on like a river , righteousness like a never-failing stream ! " ) . This theological lens powerfully bolsters their plea for a just peace , urging interlocutors to understand the conflict not merely as territorial but as involving deep , existential questions of identity , inherent human dignity , and divine justice . <p> Furthermore , Palestinian Christian theological discourse often emphasizes the profound importance of nonviolence and peace-making , rooted in the biblical commands to love and reconciliation -- attributes that are absolutely essential for any long-term , sustainable resolution . Such perspectives help to significantly enlarge the scope of theological dialogue , urging Christian communities worldwide to engage in robust advocacy for a peace that genuinely respects the human rights and inherent dignity of all involved , regardless of their background . Mitri Raheb 's ( 2014 ) work , for instance , offers a powerful articulation @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ transforming theological insights into a blueprint for resistance and reconciliation . The Kairos Palestine document ( 2009 ) serves as a collective prophetic voice , urging the global church to stand in solidarity with the oppressed and to reject theological justifications for political injustice . <p> The Imperative for a Just and Inclusive Discourse <p> Jamie Glazov 's essay , " Tucker Carlson 's Lies About Israel , " ultimately reveals itself not as a balanced defence of truth , but as a sophisticated polemic designed to insulate a specific political project from meaningful scrutiny by elevating the discourse to a fabricated theological and moral high ground . By employing rhetoric that demonizes the perceived opponent ( " death cult " ) , selectively uses and distorts religious texts ( hermeneutical violence ) , and attempts to mobilize an exclusionary theological vision ( Christian Zionism ) , the essay actively violates the fundamental principles of justice , interreligious inclusion , and global peace . The Palestinian Christian perspective , with its unwavering commitment to a theology of liberation and justice , provides the most essential and bold critical discourse against @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ a true and lasting peace can not be found in a theology that justifies political oppression , nor through a discourse that denies the full humanity and agency of the " other . " A truly scholarly , academic , and moral analysis must move beyond the simplistic , polemical accusation of " lies " to courageously confront the foundational issues of justice , equity , and human dignity . The pressing question Glazov poses about Carlson 's motivations -- " What does all of this say about the real impulses and yearnings that motivate and inspire Mr. Carlson ? " -- is far more productively and ethically applied to Glazov 's own essay , revealing impulses deeply rooted in political defence and theological exclusion . <p> A Palestinian Christian hermeneutical reading redeems the humanity that Glazov 's essay so aggressively erases . It insists that genuine peace can not emerge from demonology or caricature , but only from profound truth , sincere repentance , and mutual recognition of the other 's sacred dignity . The real theological challenge is not whether Israel or Palestine aligns perfectly with eschatological prophecy @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ collectively embody the divine command to love the neighbour -- including the perceived enemy . A just discourse must acknowledge all suffering without hierarchy and condemn all violence without selectivity . The path forward lies in shared redemption , not triumphalism . In this expansive vision , both the cross and the crescent can point toward a universal liberation -- the liberation of all humanity from the corrosive forces of fear , hatred , and falsehood , toward a common table where justice and mercy converge . <p> Glazov 's polemic against Tucker Carlson is ultimately less a defence of Israel than it is an apologia for ideological blindness . Its demonization of Islam , instrumentalization of Christian theology , and erasure of Palestinian suffering tragically reproduce the very patterns of enmity that sustain global conflict . A hermeneutics of justice -- informed by the Quranic ethic of mercy , the prophetic vision of the Hebrew Bible , and the Gospel 's radical love -- compels us to dismantle such narratives . Continued or intensified fighting in Gaza , escalation in the West Bank , and a growing risk of spillover into neighbouring states are key dangers in the region , according to CFR . <p> Examining the Israel -- Iran -- Lebanon triangle , the survey warned of direct @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ as escalation involving Hezbollah in Lebanon . Attacks on energy , military , or strategic infrastructure are possible in this interconnected set of conflicts , which CFR considers both highly likely and highly impactful , making it the single most dangerous theatre . <h> Russia -- Ukraine : A grinding war that would continue into 2026 <p> CFR placed the Russia -- Ukraine war in the top Tier I , with expectations of continued large-scale fighting , possible territorial shifts , and pressure towards a ceasefire that could lock in gains for Russia . The conflict 's impact would extend beyond Europe , affecting global energy markets , food security , NATO cohesion , and great-power rivalry , the survey noted . <h> From North Korea to the South China Sea and Taiwan : East Asia on the boil <p> North Korea remains a Tier I concern , with provocations such as missile tests , nuclear escalation , or military clashes carrying catastrophic potential if they draw the US , South Korea , or Japan into a wider conflict . <p> The South China Sea and Taiwan are listed under @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ , particularly the Philippines , are possible in 2026 . Escalating pressure on Taiwan driven by Chinese territorial ambitions could fall short of full-scale war , but still prove deeply destabilising for the region . <h> American challenges : From conflict with Venezuela to violence in Haiti <p> Venezuela presents an extreme scenario of direct US military escalation and is listed as a Tier I contingency by the survey . The likelihood of a full-scale war is assessed as lower , but the potential impact would be very high . <p> Internal violence and governance collapse in Mexico and Haiti appear in Tier II , reflecting concerns about migration pressures , criminal violence , and state fragility near US borders . <h> Cyberwar : Another war front of the future <p> Strikingly , Tier I contingencies include the possibility of a severe cyberattack on US critical infrastructure . This could target power grids , communications , or financial systems , carried out by state or state-linked actors , with cascading economic and political effects . <p> For the US , the survey also highlighted rising concerns about domestic political violence @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ risk calculations . <h> Africa 's most likely wars with the least attention <p> Sudan conflict is among the most likely to worsen in 2026 , though it is listed under Tier III due to limited US strategic impact . Similar dynamics apply to conflicts in Somalia , the Democratic Republic of Congo , and the Sahel states . These crises , according to CFR , could lead to severe humanitarian catastrophes while remaining largely out of sustained global focus . <h> A world harder to stabilise <p> CFR reached the stark conclusion that 2026 is likely to be more violent and more fragmented than previous years , with conflicts overlapping and mutually reinforcing one another . <p> While preventive diplomacy could avert some crises , political will and resources for conflict prevention are shrinking , it noted .
